newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish tax could hit shares, help foreign buyers.
newsitem.headline: Danish tax could hit shares, help foreign buyers.

text.p: A tentative government proposal to tax yields of pension-related shareholdings could slash stock prices across the board but provide a windfall for tax-exempted foreign investors, industry executives said on Tuesday.

"The introduction of a real-yield tax will mean a fall in stock market prices of at least five percent," Niels Hougaard, investment manager of Kommunernes Pensionforsikringsselskab pension fund, told Danish financial daily Borsen on Tuesday.
Plans to introduce such a levy, already applied to bonds, were raised during an abortive government attempt to win support from the Conservative opposition for its 1997 budget.

The scheme, still unofficial and far from assured of broader political support, would tax the yields of shares held by pension funds, insurance companies or as part of private pension plans, in order to finance a cut in corporation tax.
"Danish institutional investors will look for the same returns after tax, which means that prices will fall. This will be a chance for foreign investors to buy Danish shares cheaply," Hougaard said.
He added that he saw the Copenhagen All-Share Index, which closed on Monday at 442.20, falling below 420 three months after the introduction of such a tax.
Jesper Nielsen, of brokerage Den Koebenhavnske Boers, told Borsen that the mere prospect of the levy would dampen trade.
"A real-yield tax is a screw that the government can turn according to its need for revenue. This uncertainty will not have a positive effect on the market," he said.
The possibility of a tax is already cited by dealers as weighing on stock and bond prices over the past few days.
Government planners say that the negative effects of the levy would be offset by growth stimulated by the accompanying cut in company tax.
